title: Ethics, permission, scope and rules of engagement
subtitle: Learn written authorization, scope boundaries, safe methods, evidence handling and reporting.
description: Learn written authorization, scope boundaries, safe methods, evidence handling and reporting. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 1 — Ethics, permission, scope and rules of engagement

LEARNING OUTCOME
Learn written authorization, scope boundaries, safe methods, evidence handling and reporting.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Ethical hacking is a controlled assessment performed for a system owner under explicit authorization. Curiosity, a public IP address, an exposed login page or a person’s employer is not permission. Before testing, obtain written authorization, identify exact targets and dates, list allowed and prohibited actions, agree on data handling and document a stop condition.

blocks.text: A useful scope states assets, testing windows, test accounts, data limits, rate limits, third-party boundaries and reporting contacts. Never expand to a related domain, another tenant or a personal account because it appears connected. If scope is unclear, stop and request clarification.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Safety guardrail. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Data handling. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Use synthetic data, avoid collecting credentials, do not attempt persistence or destructive actions, redact evidence and notify the owner if a serious issue or accidental exposure appears. Never try to obtain private information about a suspected person.

Visual 6/6 — Report path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.output: Written scope is the boundary that tells a tester when to stop.

blocks.question: Before Lesson 1 testing, what should be confirmed?
options: A friend said it is okay
The exact target is covered by written permission
blocks.explanation: Written permission should define target and allowed methods.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: How should a finding from Lesson 1 be handled?
options: Save minimal redacted evidence and report through the approved channel
Include a real password as proof
blocks.explanation: Findings need scoped, protected and reproducible evidence.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What requires the learner to stop?
options: A lab result needs an explanation
Target is out of scope or testing may cause unexpected harm
blocks.explanation: Stop if scope or safety limits may be crossed.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.
